articles.text: The 12th annual Piedmont School Maker Faire turned the Piedmont High School campus into a Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts & Math (S.T.E.A.M.) carnival on Sunday, May 17. Around 1,000 guests attended the 2026 iteration of the event, which unleashed the creative minds of kids and adults to fabricate and build. Perennial favorites like the Nerdy Derby grabbed the attention of attendees, inspiring them to engineer vehicles to withstand the spectacular ramp spanning the height of the amphitheater. At the other end of campus budding engineers tested their ingenuity at the Maker River by modifying small vessels of cork, rubber and wood for trial runs down the handcrafted aqueduct. The event included popular hands-on exhibits like Air Rockets and LEGOS with novel attractions, including the Mini Golf Links, a rustic apple press, and workshops for crafting jewelry. Piedmont became the first school district in the nation to host an official K-12 School Maker Faire in 2014. Dave Ragones, co-founded Piedmont Makers in 2014 with Piedmonter Vince Monical. The first recorded Maker Faire took place in San Mateo in 2006. The apex of the Makers program is Team 8033, Highlander Robotics, which competes in the World Championships for a global title year after year. The 2024 robot Banshee was active on the patio in the Fabrication Laboratory, while the current 2026 robot Wisp, was on the workbench inside in the shop for inspections and a Q & A with team members. Team 8033 also offered demonstrations of the Fab Lab’s laser cutter, quickly transforming digital blueprints into wooden keepsakes. Co-Presidents of Piedmont Makers Kevin Clark and Ben Stein have been at the helm of Makers since Ragones’ transitioned to Treasurer a year ago. articles.text: Editor: I moved to Piedmont when I was seven years old. Before that, I spent my entire childhood in Montclair, where I attended Montclair Elementary for TK, kindergarten, and first grade. I had a wonderful experience at Montclair Elementary—I loved my teachers and made great memories. However, my parents were concerned about the middle school and high school options available to me. They wanted me to build friendships in elementary school that would last through high school. Since I had cousins in Piedmont who attended Beach Elementary, my parents decided it was best for us to move here and join its schools. When I began second grade at Beach Elementary, I was warmly welcomed by some of the most supportive teachers I could imagine! I quickly made a lot of new friends, and I’m still close with many of them today. Our move to Piedmont wasn’t just about finding friends and a sense of community; it was also about the exceptional education offered by the public schools. I have had amazing teachers every year, and I feel fortunate for the classes and resources available to us. I know that Piedmont schools continue to thrive thanks to the community’s commitment to funding what truly matters. That’s why I strongly urge everyone to vote YES on Measure H. Without it, we risk losing 20% of our school funding, which is vital for our resources, teachers, and community. Please make your voice heard and vote YES! –Hazel Schaeffer

articles.text: The eight Alameda County local ballot measures scheduled for the June 2, 2026 Primary Election were evaluated in April 2026 by a Ballot Watchdog group of evaluators from the non-profit and nonpartisan Alameda County Civil Grand Jurors’ Association (ACCGJA). The measures’ titles were evaluated for accuracy and fairness pursuant to the California Elections Code and the criteria established by the association for each type of ballot measure, e.g. Bond Measure, Tax Measure and Other (non-tax measure). This review by the ACCGJA is unrelated to the current sitting Civil Grand Jury; it is also unrelated to the California Civil Grand Jurors’ Association, the Alameda County Registrar of Voters, and the County of Alameda. The collective ratings represent the average score arrived at by the evaluators who are Association members and are all former grand jury members. The scoring system is comparable to the popular “Yelp” type scoring system (a score of one is worst; five is best). Like a Yelp evaluation, the ratings reflect the average of the evaluators’ educated opinions, based on the established criteria as to what should, and should not, be included in each type of ballot measure. We emphasize that the ACCGJA IS NOT evaluating the merits of the proposed measures. The evaluation is not partisan - neither liberal nor conservative. We are only concerned with the accuracy and impartiality of the 75-word ballot title being put to the voters. Those 75 words are the only thing that we know every voter sees as they vote. State law requires ballot language to be “a true and impartial synopsis of the purpose of the proposed measure and shall be in language that is neither argumentative nor likely to create prejudice for or against the measure.” Unfortunately, many jurisdictions disregard the intent of the law by exaggerating the benefits and glossing over the costs, as well as by adding extraneous verbiage designed to favor passage of the measure. No one, other than the agency promoting the measure, is required to approve the agency’s language. To counteract this, there is a growing need for citizens to actively and consistently monitor and evaluate local governments’ ballot descriptions. This current ACCGJA effort supports the findings of the 2021 Alameda County Civil Grand Jury report, The Need for Accuracy and Impartiality of Ballot Measure Questions. Additional information can be found on the Ballot Watchdog group website: https://ballotwatchdog.com/ most of the measures exhibited some degree of proponent bias, emphasizing the benefits and glossing over the costs, meaning the authors want the measure to pass. While that tilt may be understandable, it is not in compliance with the law. Results: The Ballot Watchdog review produced individual ballot measure scores ranging from 1.8 to 4.2. The average was 3.5. The most common issue that caused a reduction in the score from the maximum of 5 was a lack of clarity as to the intent and need for the measure. Another common problem for tax measures was the lack of where and how this new tax relates to the other existing taxes or bonded indebtedness of that jurisdiction. For example, a proposed tax measure may fail to mention what the existing tax rate is, or whether the new tax or bond was being added to an existing similar tax or bond. Thus, voters could not learn the amount of increase or even the percentage of increase if the proposed measure were to pass. Also common was the inclusion of extraneous verbiage designed to influence a favorable vote on the measure, such as emphasizing popular or feel-good spending categories that might be improved if the measure were to pass. articles.text: Lisa Troseth, practitioner of Christian Science healing and international speaker, will present her talk, “Moving past fear - to healing,” on Saturday, May 23, at 2:30 p.m., at the Orinda Library Auditorium. The talk will focus on universal healing precepts found in the Holy Bible, especially in Christ Jesus’ life and teachings, showing how they are available for anyone to understand and experience through the lens of Christian Science. “Fear can be overcome and even healed in our lives by discovering the strong connection and relationship we have to something bigger than ourselves—God,” says Troseth. “By learning to lean and rely on this greater, higher good, we can feel moved to love beyond ourselves—and this frees us from fear and so much more.” Troseth has been a Christian Science practitioner for many years, helping people on a daily basis through this scientific approach to prayer. She travels from her home base in Nyack, New York, to speak to audiences around the world as a member of the Christian Science Board of Lectureship. The talk is free, open to the community, and jointly sponsored by First Church of Christ, Scientist, Orinda and First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland.

articles.text: Misha is an 8-year-old Siamese mix with the soul of a cozy old friend. She’s happiest spending quiet days near her person—lounging nearby while you work, accepting head scratches, or curling up across your legs for cuddles. Although she’s shy with strangers, Misha warms up with patience and consistency and thrives in a calm, predictable home. Someone gentle and observant will quickly discover her adorable sassy side if meals are running late, as well as her love for being brushed, heating pads, and sweet petting sessions. While she does require ongoing care for arthritis, including a monthly injection at the vet, Misha still has a playful side, too! Her favorite activity is batting enthusiastically at a rainbow ribbon wand toy, sometimes scrambling in circles or trying to catch it with her toothless little mouth. Her bursts of play are short Adopt Misha through Cat Town. and senior-style, but they’re full of personality! For someone looking for a mellow, affectionate friend with a deeply comforting presence, Misha’s the kind of gal you don’t want to miss out on. She’ll make your house feel like a home. Misha is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www.cattownoakland. org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: The Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival returns on Saturday, June 20, 2026, from 12:00 - 6:00 p.m., bringing together the best of local craft beverages, live entertainment, and community spirit for a lively summer celebration. Presented by the Montclair Village Association, this popular street festival will feature over 50 craft beverage tastings, including beer, wine, cider, and alcohol-free options, alongside delicious offerings from local chefs and artisan vendors. In addition to tastings, the festival offers free musical performances by local favorites – Prospect, Cardboard People, Bululú, DJ BlackWoman, and DJ2 – hosted by Candi Martinez throughout the day on the Mister Beever’s Paws & Claws Stage powered by Meet Your Core Pilates. articles.text: It wasn’t until 1610, when Galileo Galilei discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter, that humans learned there were moons other than our own. We know now that the Moon is just one of more than 891 moons in our entire solar system. However, our Moon is unique because it belongs to the only planet in our solar system that has life. As our closest neighbor in space, the Moon has given scientists incredible insight on both Earth and our solar system. Lunar missions conducted by NASA over the years have allowed humans to peek into our solar system’s past, long before we were ever around. In knowing more about our solar system’s past, we gain greater context of Earth’s place in our solar system. The Start Although there are varying theories about the Moon’s origin, it is widely agreed that a powerful and massive collision was the genesis event. It is theorized that approximately 4.5 billion years ago, an object about the size of Mars collided with Earth. The large and violent collision between the two objects sent molten and vaporized debris out into space. Over time, the materials from the collision formed the Moon. In the 60s and 70s, the Apollo program helped strengthen scientists’ existing theories about the Moon. The discoveries from NASA’s Apollo program helped transform existing theories about the start of the Moon. During the Apollo missions, lunar rock samples were collected and analyzed. These samples gave scientists incredible answers to long-standing questions. They could determine from the samples that during the Moon’s formation it had been molten and for millions of years it had been covered with magma. Scientists also learned that lunar rocks and Earth rocks have an incredibly similar chemical composition. The chemical composition of the two is so similar that scientists were able to conclude that the Moon had once been a part of Earth. The findings from the Apollo missions gave scientists context for future theNASA Artemis II at the pad with a full Snow Moon ories and discoveries about the Moon and our solar system. A planet full of history Every crater on the Moon tells us a story about our solar system’s past. Asteroids, meteoroids, and comets have marked the surface of the Moon for millions of years, leaving a vast history for us to explore. There is no wind or liquid water on the Moon, preserving the impact craters on the surface. Meanwhile, impact evidence on Earth has been affected by erosion, plate tectonics, and volcanic activity. By investigating the Moon’s craters, we learn more about both the Moon’s and our solar system’s past. The more scientists learn about the Moon’s craters, the better insight astronauts will have when they visit the Moon in the future. The Artemis program NASA’s Artemis program has opened the door to further investigation into the Moon and beyond. Through a series of missions, scientists will have greater insight into questions surrounding the Moon and what to expect for and from future lunar missions. In the most recent phase, Artemis II, astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen performed various tasks during their journey; analyzing and recording geologic features of the Moon. The information gained from Artemis II will help scientists develop a better geologic history of the Moon and will be crucial for future exploration of the Moon and eventually Mars. Chabot’s historic telescopes As we head into warmer weather in the Bay, there will be more opportunities to clearly view celestial objects in the night sky. Since 1883, Chabot’s inception, telescope viewings have been open and free to the public. We continue that longstanding tradition every Friday and Saturday night from 7:30PM-10:30PM (weather permitting). Our incredible telescope operators and volunteers are always eager to help answer any astronomical curiosities and questions. Visit chabotspace.org to find out more information about our 3 historic telescopes: Leah, Rachel and Nellie! Keep that #MoonJoy alive Chabot has a summer full of exploration and joy planned – and there’s something for everyone! From Sci-Fi Movie Nights in the Planetarium and Hike & Sips through the redwoods, the return of Space Week to Cosmic Camp-in sleepovers under the stars. Cameron Schneider is a staff member of Chabot Space and Science Center in the Oakland hills.

We know now that the Moon is just one of more than 891 moons in our entire solar system. However, our Moon is unique because it belongs to the only planet in our solar system that has life. As our closest neighbor in space, the Moon has given scientists incredible insight on both Earth and our solar system. Lunar missions conducted by NASA over the years have allowed humans to peek into our solar system’s past, long before we were ever around. In knowing more about our solar system’s past, we gain greater context of Earth’s place in our solar system. The Start Although there are varying theories about the Moon’s origin, it is widely agreed that a powerful and massive collision was the genesis event. It is theorized that approximately 4.5 billion years ago, an object about the size of Mars collided with Earth. The large and violent collision between the two objects sent molten and vaporized debris out into space. Over time, the materials from the collision formed the Moon. In the 60s and 70s, the Apollo program helped strengthen scientists’ existing theories about the Moon. The discoveries from NASA’s Apollo program helped transform existing theories about the start of the Moon. During the Apollo missions, lunar rock samples were collected and analyzed. These samples gave scientists incredible answers to long-standing questions. They could determine from the samples that during the Moon’s formation it had been molten and for millions of years it had been covered with magma. Scientists also learned that lunar rocks and Earth rocks have an incredibly similar chemical composition. The chemical composition of the two is so similar that scientists were able to conclude that the Moon had once been a part of Earth. Asteroids, meteoroids, and comets have marked the surface of the Moon for millions of years, leaving a vast history for us to explore. articles.text: Ted Eisemon, and Theo Ferguson The Hungteetsepoppi Lodge of the Order of the Arrow (OA) held its semi-annual Ordeal and Induction of new members on March 27-29 at Camp Augusta, near Nevada City in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. Founded in 1915, the Order of the Arrow is the honor society of Scouting America (formerly the Boy Scouts of America), led by youths age 21 and under with adult advisors. Each Scouting council has its own lodge. Members are Scouts who exemplify the Scout Oath and Law and are elected by each troop. The Ordeal tests candidates’ character and commitment to the Scout Oath and Law. Scouts spend Friday night and Saturday reflecting on the meaning of service and labor on camp projects such as constructing benches, spreading wood chips, and laying out a labyrinth for summer camp activities. The Induction was held Saturday evening in the forest. For their exemplary service and leadership, Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson and former Lodge Vice Chief Drew Kobal were elevated to Vigil members, the highest honor in the OA. According to Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson, one thing that makes the OA unique is that it is a completely youth-driven organization. Theo is now serving his second term as Lodge Chief. The organization also provides many experiences across the nation. Theo regularly travels across California to attend planning meetings and teaches at national training events. He said that being Lodge Chief has “transformed [his] leadership and organizational abilities,” and that his favorite part has been “meeting hundreds of amazing and inspiring people from all over, creating an awesome network of peers.” Lodge Advisor Bryan Gros said that the Hungteetsepoppi Lodge has been providing service to Camp Augusta for decades. Some of the recent projects involve repairing structures that the Lodge installed years ago. Many youth spent a week or two at the camp when they were younger and really enjoyed returning to camp as Scouts. The Lodge also helps support Piedmont Scouting by assisting with the Cub program and setting up the annual Tree Lot. Adult Scout leaders may become OA members. Jen Gregovich, who is a member of the Board of Directors of Camp Augusta, as well as Troop 15 Scoutmaster, and her daughter, Abigail Gregovich, went through the Ordeal and were inducted. Council Member at Large and former Lodge Advisor Kevin Fischer and Steve Sciamanna, boyhood friends as Scouts in Troop 6, have continued their friendship and service as adult Scout leaders and OA members. Jim Mehlinger began Scouting more than seven decades ago in a troop formed by his grandfather more than a century ago. He has been an OA member for almost seven decades and participated in the induction of his grandson, Ted Eisemon. articles.text: On Monday, May 18, the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) hosted a community event at the brand new Ellis Family Pavilion at the Piedmont Community Pool. PEF Community Engagement Chairs Molly Lloyd, Sarah Pearson, and Rich Thompson, welcomed “empty nesters” to an evening of margaritas, light bites, and the opportunity to connect with each other. About 60 community members attended the reception and were encouraged to drop by the AP Art Exhibit at Piedmont High School which was being held at the same time. “It is a common misconception that PUSD only serves families with current students,” said Thompson. “In reality, our schools offer cultural and athletic experiences for the entire city that enrich the Piedmont community.” During his remarks, Thompson shared that PEF was pleased to host enjoyable community events. “All we ask in return is that when PEF comes knocking, you respond generously,” he concluded. The heart of town buzzed with activity, with open houses at the middle and high schools, community group meetings, and families enjoying the warm day at the pool, creating a vibrant backdrop for the event. PEF continues to create meaningful opportunities for all community members to stay connected and support Piedmont schools, helping ensure that current and future generations receive an exceptional educational experience. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team continues its strong performance in the North Coast Section postseason. On Saturday, May 16 at the NCS Bayshore Area Championships, the Highlanders qualified for the prestigious Meet of Champions in 13 events by gaining a top-six finish or qualifying time. “The jump from WACC to Bayshore is one that teaches us a lot about ourselves, where we go from 12 teams up to 34 and welcome elite competition,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. “Of our 40 athletes that competed yesterday, 17 will move on either as individuals or in relays.” It was a big afternoon for junior sprinter Claire Aubrecht, who qualified to the Meet of Champions individually in the 100 meter dash and 200-meter. She was also a part of the 4x100 and 4x400 relay teams reaching the next stage. In the 100, Aubrecht clocked a time of 12.45 seconds to place seventh of 21. She met the exact time needed to qualify for the Meet of Champions. As for the 200, she finished fifth of 23 in 25.59. Both were personal best times resulting in lowering the school’s record time in each Avedis Gourjian placed third of 13 in the pole vault at the NCS Bayshore Area Championships. Malia Williams placed third in the high jump at the NCS Bayshore. Staff Photos Claire Aubrecht qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions in four events at the NCS Bayshore Area Championships. event. She was the second leg in the 4x100 relay team which posted a time of 49.21 seconds with teammates Akunna Iroh, Darcy McKee, and Nia Jackson. The team placed 2nd of 19 teams. It was another record time for the school. The 4x400 team of Aubrecht, Skylar Best, Daniela Lucaccini, and Iroh placed fifth of 11 in 4:17.39. “Claire qualified to MOC in four events, including pushing her 100m and 200m record breaking times down further, and being a part of the 4x100 that crushed last year’s all-time record breaking time by over a half second,” Assadi said. It was also a strong day for junior Sebastien Swain who reached the Meet of Champions in two events. He was second in a field of 24 runners in the 800 meters with a time of 1:56.46. He was also part of the 4x400 relay team with Rehan Mumtaz, Ben Gerber, and Maddox Ma which placed second of 18 schools with a time of 3:25.02. “Seb took second in the open 8 and was a part of the second place 4x4. Their time is the fastest since the CIF qualifying team in 2023, and was the fastest 4x4 time we’ve ever run at Bayshore,” Assadi said. articles.text: First Piedmont team to medal at State Piedmont High’s boys’ 200 medley relay team of Nik Costello, Asher Takazawa, Connor Carnazzo, and Jeffrey Latronica made school history at the 2026 CIF State Championships at Clovis West High School. It placed ninth overall out of 18 finalists and 40 total schools in California with a time of 1:33.56. They became the only relay team in PHS history to finish with a top-9 medal in the State meet’s 12-year history. It is also the first time the school had two teams as finalists after the 400 team reached its B Finals. Costello replaced usual breaststroker Cole Carnazzo on the 200 medley team, enabling Latronica to swim the last leg. Carnazzo, had an AP test and could not make it to the state meet. “This required us to switch the order so that our typical freestyler, Nik Costello, swam breaststroke. This season proved to be challenging without having a home pool to practice in, we swam at four different locations. I am excited to see what next year will bring; hopefully we will make it to states again,” coach Elizabeth Dally said. Piedmont’s 400 freestyle team featured Dimitri Secor replacing Takazawa and placing 16th in 3:07.91. It marked back-to-back appearances for Piedmont’s boys’ relay teams to reach State after last year’s 200 medley and 400 freestyle teams reached the preliminary round to finish 23rd and 21st respectively. Costello and Takazawa were both members of that group. “The whole team put in a lot of work to get faster. When we went into NCS with the No. 1 seed we knew we could get to State. We didn’t expect to get top-nine and be in the A Final. I’m really proud of our team,” Costello said. “We were going into this not expecting this at all. It was our goal to make top-three at NCS and wound up getting fourth. That podium was not expected at all. One thing we did really well this year was push the team bonding and how much trust we had in each other. There was a lot of togetherness in our team,” Takazawa said Nik Costello (left), Asher Takazawa, Connor Carnazzo, and Jeffrey Latronica made school history by finishing ninth in the 200 medley relays at the CIF State Swimming Championships. To reach the finals, the 200 team qualified by finishing ninth of 40 in 1:32.58. In the final, Takazawa clocked 23.97 seconds in the back stroke, Costello had a 26.22 breast stroke, Carnazzo had a 22.55 butterfly, while Latronica swam freestyle of 20.82. In the 400 free preliminary round, they finished 17th of 40 with a time of 3:07.23. Both Carnazzo and Latronica are freshmen. “Those two guys are fast. They are going to do many good things in the future. Jeffrey really stepped up and Connor has put on a show since WACC. It’s been great to see the young guys pop off,” Costello said of the newcomers. “I’ve known Connor and Jeffrey for so long, it’s been super cool seeing their growth. It’s amazing how they stepped up and took matters into their own hands. What they did really well was trusting the process, they depended on us to explain how the season goes, and showed up to race and perform when they needed to,” Takazawa added. The Highlanders’ swimming team now has sent at least one athlete to the CIF State Championships four out of the last five years. Simon Lins competed in the 50 freestyle and 100 backstroke in 2022, Nina Schwab featured in the one-meter dive in 2024, while the 200 medley and 400 freestyle boys’ relay teams have now qualified in 2025 and 2026. And with Costello and Secor being the only graduating seniors Piedmont’s 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams qualified for the State swim meet, Pictured are Jeffrey Latronica (left), Asher Takazawa, Connor Carnazzo, Nik Costello, and Dimitri Secor.

articles.text: Staff Photos Joey Assalian helped reel in a 6-3, 6-4 win at No. 1 doubles against San Ramon Valley. Piedmont High’s boys’ tennis team’s season came to an end on Tuesday, May 12. As the No. 12 seed in the Division 1 North Coast Section Team Tournament, Piedmont fell by a score of 4-2 to No. 5 San Ramon Valley on the Wolves’ home court in Danville. The Highlanders end their season with a 16-7 overall record, while Lucas Smolko secured the school’s only boys’ NCS Individual singles title since Barry Gilbert in 1975. “We had a really good season. We finished second in the Western Alameda County Conference and had a 16-7 win-loss record. Plus, Lucas won the NCS D2 singles title, the first for the Piedmont boys in over 50 years,” said coach Jim Landes. Piedmont won the first two matches of the day to take an early 2-0 lead, but SRV roared back to win the next four matches to clinch the match. At No. 1 doubles, Ben Davis and Joey Assalian won 6-3, 6-4. After that, Carter Brookfield and Hunter Fasteau won 7-6 (7-4), 6-4 at No. 2 doubles. “Joey and Ben played really well and won in straight sets. Hunter and Carter won the first set in a tiebreak and then cruised to a victory in the second,” Landes said. After that, Nate Welch lost 6-3, 6-1 at No. 2 singles and Ari Moskovitz fell 6-0, 6-1 at the No. 3 spot. Then, Travers Kemp and Henry van den Bos lost at No. 3 doubles 7-5, 6-4 to give the Wolves a 3-2 advantage. The last two matches on the courts were Emilio Misra at No. 4 singles and Smolko in the top singles match. Smolko won the first set 7-6 (7-4) but lost 6-3 in the second. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company presents the West Coast premiere of Pictures from Home, a stage adaptation of photographer Larry Sultan’s memoir about family and memory, running now through May 31 at Marin Theatre in Mill Valley. Adapted by playwright Sharr White and directed by Jonathan Moscone, the production follows Sultan as he documents and interviews his parents over more than a decade, revisiting family stories and tensions while searching for a deeper understanding of his upbringing. The play is based on Sultan’s landmark photo memoir and premiered on Broadway at Studio 54 starring Nathan Lane, Danny Burstein and Zoë Wanamaker. Bay Area actor Victor Talmadge stars as Irving Sultan alongside Daniel Cantor as Larry Sultan and Susan Koozin as Jean Sultan. Talmadge, making his Marin Theatre debut, has appeared in touring productions of “The King & I” and “The Lion King,” as well as in David Mamet’s “November” on Broadway. Cantor previously appeared at Marin Theatre in “Waste” and performed on Broadway in “Leopoldstadt.” Koozin previously played Jean Sultan in a production at Alley Theatre in Houston. articles.text: Maren Hassinger Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing, the comprehensive retrospective to date of the artist’s body of work, opens at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) June 6. The exhibition features half a century of work by Hassinger, including large-scale sculpture, site-specific installation, video, and performance, and will display more than twenty of her most notable works from the 1970s to the present. Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing will be accompanied by an extensive exhibition catalogue, featuring new scholarly essays and previously unpublished documentation of her artwork. Notable displayed works include Love (2008), a site-specific sculpture composed of pink plastic bags inflated by human breath and filled with love notes; Beach (1980), a floor installation consisting of plaster and wooden dowels; and multiple sculptures that incorporate recently harvested tree branches which BAMPFA showcases in partnership with the University of California Botanical Garden. “Maren Hassinger’s practice has been of great influence for generations of artists,” Chief Curator Margot Norton said in a press release. “We are thrilled to finally bring her artworks and their stories from across her career together through our exhibition, and to showcase Hassinger’s profound contributions to contemporary art.” “Maren Hassinger’s work invites us to reflect on the beauty and complexity of human connection, through movement, material, and shared experience,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director, Julie Rodrigues Widholm. “Presenting this landmark retrospective at BAMPFA underscores our commitment to amplifying artists whose practices challenge conventions and inspire collective engagement across generations.” The retrospective will be on display at BAMPFA June 6 through November 29. More information about this and other public programs can be found at bampfa.org.
articles.title: Maren Hassinger Retrospective opens at BAMPFA next month

articles.text: Concert lotteries open now online Stern Grove Festival returns to San Francisco this summer with a mix of internationally recognized performers and local artists. The 2026 season is scheduled to run from June 14 through August 16 at Sigmund Stern Recreation Grove. Headliners include Al Green, Public Enemy, Patti LaBelle, and Major Lazer. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception, the organization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites.The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater, and music. articles.text: An exhibition showcasing the artistry of Lawrence Ferlinghetti, one of San Francisco’s most significant cultural figures, is now on view at the Legion of Honor. Ferlinghetti (1919 - 2021) was a poet, activist, publisher, and co-founder of the famous City Lights Bookstore in San Francisco, the epicenter of the Beat generation of writers. The independent bookstore is considered a literary landmark and has been a gathering space for writers since Ferlinghetti founded the store in 1955 with the now-famous Pocket Poets Series. Since then the press has gone on to publish a wide range of titles, including poetry and prose, fiction and nonfiction, international and local authors. Ferlinghetti was also an avid painter, draftsman, and printmaker, and his work across mediums often combines image and text exploring themes of isolation, violence, and human resilience. With artworks drawn entirely from the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s works on paper collection, this exhibition showcases Ferlinghetti’s work in printmaking, including etching, lithography, and letterpress. The exhibition is on view now through July 19. For more information, visit https://www. famsf.org/exhibitions/ferlinghetti-san-francisco. Lawrence Ferlinghetti
articles.title: Ferlinghetti exhibition on view at Legion of Honor through July

articles.text: Installation view of Monet and Venice The de Young Museum presents Monet and Venice, the first major international loan exhibition devoted to Claude Monet’s paintings of Venice, on view now through July 26. Co-organized by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and the Brooklyn Museum, the exhibition features more than 100 works, including more than 20 of Monet’s 37 Venice canvases, including his iconic Water Lilies. Monet and Venice is the first exhibition dedicated to Monet’s Venetian paintings since their debut in Paris over a century ago. The exhibition centers on Monet’s only visit to Venice, Photo courtesy of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco which took place in 1908 when the artist was 68 years old. According to organizers, the trip marked Monet’s final major international journey and his last sustained focus on architectural subjects. “Although Monet visited Venice only once, his paintings of the city are among his most dazzling,” Thomas P. Campbell, director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, said in a press release. “Unlike bustling scenes painted by other artists, Monet’s Venice is hauntingly deserted, with its architecture, buildings, and canals dissolving in an atmospheric light.” Works by Monet will be lent by institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, along with private collections. The exhibition will also include works by artists associated with Venice, including Canaletto, John Singer Sargent, J. M. W. Turner and James McNeill Whistler. “His Venetian paintings are among the most luminous and poetic of his career,” added Melissa E. Buron, exhibition co-curator and director of collections and chief curator at the Victoria and Albert Museum. “His time in Venice was a critical period of creative renewal that has not previously been explored in-depth before this exhibition.” For more information, visit https://www.famsf.org/.
articles.title: Monet and Venice exhibit now on view at de Young Museum

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s newest exhibition, UNBOUND: Art, Blackness, and the Universe, is now on view. UNBOUND is a unique group exhibition that explores connections between Blackness and spiritual cosmologies. Organized by Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, the community retrospective highlights the similarities between the Black existence and “cosmic Blackness,” or Afrofuturism. UNBOUND includes paintings, glass sculptures, and installations celebrating the modern artistic genre. The exhibition features artists David Alabo, Renee Cox, Oasa DuVerney, Torkwase Dyson, Allison Janae Hamilton, Barkley L. Hendricks, Cullen B. Washington Jr., M. Carmen Lane and Sidra Bell, Michi Meko, Gustavo Nazareno, Rashaad Newsome, Chris Ofili, Mikael Owunna, Harmonia Rosales, Lorna Simpson, Didier William, and Fred Wilson. “For the past twenty years, MoAD has proudly embarked on a journey to ensure that Black creative expression is embraced, elevated, and seen by international visitors and those that call the Bay Area home,” said Monetta White, Executive Director and CEO. “The artistic depth of UNBOUND will bring intergenerational African Diasporic voices together under an innovative curatorial framework that shifts the focus through which we understand and appreciate contemporary art.” “This exhibition is a celebration of the vast conceptual capacity of Blackness, and treats Black existence with the same imaginative and intellectual openness we apply to thinking through metaphysics and the cosmos,” Lee added. “In doing so, it makes a radical claim that Blackness is not marginal, but central to how we comprehend being, time, and the universe itself.” For more information, visit https://www.moadsf.org. Allison Janae Hamilton is one of over a dozen Black artists featured in MoAD’s UNBOUND.
articles.title: UNBOUND: Art, Blackness and the Universe now on view at MoAD

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), California’s oldest youth orchestra, will present a Pops Pre-Tour Concert, the final performance of its 2025–2026 subscription season, on Sunday, June 7 at 3:00 p.m. at The Ascension Greek Orthodox Cathedral (4700 Lincoln Avenue, Oakland). The concert will feature a vibrant audience-friendly program ranging from Americana classics to Nordic masterworks, previewing the orchestra’s upcoming international tour repertoire. The program will feature Felicia Ng, one of the winners of YPSO’s Concerto Competition, performing the first movement of Sergei Golovko’s Concerto for Marimba and Orchestra. “I chose this piece because it’s energetic, blends contemporary with classical style, and has great storytelling that is especially compelling to me,” said Ng. In preparation for YPSO’s Summer tour to Finland and Sweden, the program features the final two movements of Sibelius’s Symphony No. 1 — Movement III: Allegro and Movement IV: Finale (Quasi una Fantasia). Additional program highlights include Copland’s energetic “Buckaroo Holiday” from Rodeo and popular favorites such as Leroy Anderson’s Home Stretch and Sousa’s The Stars and Stripes Forever, continuing YPSO’s Pops concert tradition. General Admission is $20; students are free (registration is required). Box Office and Concert Info: ypsomusic.org/events. As both a season finale and a moment of recognition, the concert will honor YPSO’s graduating senior musicians, celebrating their contributions to the orchestra and their next steps as they continue their musical and academic journeys. In conjunction with the concert, YPSO will launch its annual “Spring Into Music!” Silent Auction in support of YPSO programs and student tour opportunities. The auction features experiences, dining, and unique offerings from local businesses and community supporters. Proceeds help sustain YPSO’s concerts, coaching, educational activities, chamber music, and touring opportunities Felicia Ng will perform a solo at the Pops Pre-Tour Concert. for young musicians across the Bay Area. The school’s feature performance takes place on July 14, at the Oakland Asian Cultural Center. The choir’s main goal is to share Georgian culture with different parts of the world. Over the 15 years, several international projects were accomplished, including participation and awards at the Golden Gate International Choral Festival; World Peace Choral Festival, Vienna; Canti Veris Choral Festival, Prague; Tokyo International Choral Festival; and other leading events in Idaho, Rome, Norway, Latvia, Denver, Yekaterinburg, Belarus, the UK, France, and Budapest. The choir’s concert program is very unique. It lasts for 1 hour and involves virtual traveling from the western regions of The Georgian Choir of E. Mikeladze Central Music School Georgia to the east. In their concerts, the choir performs one-totwo songs from each region with appropriate verbal presentation of the meaning, history, and musical and other differences. Therefore, the international audience is always excited and attracted by the performance. Their song-study process is very traditional. Since the choir members perform Georgian through-oral traditions, they never use music sheets during rehearsals. Instead, the choir director uses the traditional oral way of teaching. Despite international challenges and objections, the choir is active in Georgia too. It usually organizes various events and participates in local choral projects. Moreover, the choir supports the cultural exchange in Georgia. They cooperate with different organizations, including the Embassies in Georgia. articles.text: The Shawshank Redemption is an Oscar nominated film (7) that was adapted by director Frank Darabont from the Stephen King novella, Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption. The story can be found in a collection of King’s tales in the book titled Four Seasons. I have always believed that though this prolific and talented writer is most closely identified with stories of the surreal, drawn from that realm that exists beyond the evidence, he is far more. articles.text: A scene from Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse It’s often assumed that sequels, when compared to the original movie, will disappoint. It’s no small thing to create the magic displayed in the first release. But that’s definitely not the case with the animated Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, which was followed by the award-winning Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Actually, it could be argued that not only have the filmmakers found the energy of the first, but this latest incarnation is, in all respects, fresh, remarkable, and, well, seriously cool. Kids will be captivated by Across, and certainly not disappointed. In fact, the filmmakers are planning to follow Across with a third Spider-Verse thus completing what is proving, to be an extraordinary trilogy. Of course what carries both films are the familiar themes of tween/teen identity and friendship, the plot carried along at a frenetic pace by a deep bench of new characters. Of course, Spider-Man , aka Miles Morales (Shameik Moore) and Gwen Stacy aka Spider-Gwen (Hailee Seinfeld) are back for another adventure wherein they are catapulted across the universe, passing through countless portals, encountering a cohort of interesting and funny Spider-People. An example would be Spidey-Pavitr, from India (Karen Soni). There’s also an unexpected Spider Society, comprised of Spider-Men/Women, and other thing. Even a feline pet. But not to forget that back on Mile’s home turf, Brooklyn, he and Gwen confront the villainous Spot (Jason Schwartzman), a mad scientist who blows stuff up. Across the Spider-Verse offers a varied and compelling plot, powered by stunning animation, and great writing. I want the nursery I know personally, and I have always gone to,” she said. After acquiring both nurseries, it was the first time Feinberg had become a small business owner. She’s enjoyed interacting with the community. Customers Broadway Terrace Nursery’s selection of plants Jenny Feinberg in front of Broadway Terrace Nursery come in and talk to her about their gardens and what’s going on in their lives. “One of the things I really love, particularly at Broadway Terrace Nursery, it’s a lot of people’s special outing for the week,” Feinberg continued. “They look around and spend time in the nursery, and then they buy one small plant, and you just know they’ve had a great day. I’ve never had that experience in business. Because my business roles were always so remote from the customer. To have that sort of positive one-on-one experience is really fun.” But things weren’t all smooth going for her. In the opening week of the Broadway Terrace Nursery, a vehicle crashed into the storefront, running through two walls and destroying a majority of the indoor plants. What started as a celebration turned into a rebuild. “It was supposed to be this big celebration. articles.text: Fifty-four walkers and five K-9 best friends gathered at the Exedra on a lovely morning last week for a destination the group hadn’t visited in years. Zillow had listed a Piedmont home at 23 Valant Place for sale. The street name didn’t ring an immediate bell, but then it came back — the group had walked to Valant, a cul-desac off Trestle Glen Road, some years ago and never returned. Walker and real estate broker Stacey Isaacs agreed to meet the group there for a tour. Getting to Valant is not a short trip. The walkers went up Highland, Sheridan, and Wildwood Avenues, through the Hall Fenway to Crocker, up LaSalle to Indian Road — which crosses into Oakland and becomes Sunnyhills — then down the steep Bowles Place to a long set of wooden steps that drop down to Trestle Glen Road. Up that handsome street, lined with homes in a variety of architectural styles, is Valant Place. Along the way, the group talked about why 23 Valant Place has a Piedmont address at all. It is one of only two Piedmont homes on the street. The rest are in Oakland. The explanation starts in 1892, when the Piedmont Springs Hotel — a three-story white landmark and the city’s biggest tourist attraction — caught fire. Piedmont had no fire department, so Oakland’s was called. Oakland’s horses dragged a water tanker up Oakland Avenue for two hours. By the time the wagons arrived, there was nothing left to save. That fire is a big part of why Piedmont exists. In the late 1800s, Oakland launched what it called the “Greater Oakland Movement,” annexing neighboring towns and setting its sights on Piedmont. A vote on annexation was set for January 1907, but a paperwork error pushed it to March. During that window, a group of Piedmont residents filed to incorporate first. They liked Piedmont rural and undeveloped, and the burning hotel had made the case for a local fire department hard to argue with. Rallying support wasn’t easy. Historian Ann Swift has described the effort: “Hugh Craig and James Ballentine were having meetings every other night, practically trying to rally the troops.” The opposition pointed out that Piedmont had no experience with taxes, city services, or paved streets. “There was a sizable part of the city who thought there was no need to go through all that.” The incorporation vote passed. ation vote went forward in March and passed 63 to 43. Yet Piedmont was now its own city, so the vote was meaningless. Opponents tried again that September with a disincorporation election to merge with Oakland after all. That vote failed on a technicality: 92 in favor, 62 opposed, but a two-thirds majority, 102 votes, was required. Piedmont survived by 10 votes. In the rush of 1907, the new city drew its borders using the Piedmont Sanitary District’s sewer map, the most complete survey available. Sewer lines follow topography rather than streets, so the boundary zigged and zagged through neighborhoods in ways that still don’t make much geographic sense. On Valant Place, the city limit wraps around the end of the cul-de-sac to pull in numbers 22 and 23 while leaving the rest of the street in Oakland. Stacey was waiting for the group at the end of the cul-de-sac. She gave the walkers an update on the local market. While some Oakland neighborhoods have seen prices soften, Piedmont is going the other direction. The first home on Valant was built in 1932 with others following in the 1960s. Number 23, the newest, was built in 1993. Stacey called it the best current value in Piedmont. In early April a group of nine PCSC members headed to Oregon to volunteer for a nonprofit education program called The Crest, based at Willow-Witt Ranch near Ashland. The crew stayed at the ranch for six nights and slept in tents Every day the crew would work from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. with an hour break at noon, doing a variety of work with the help of David Nilson, a former PCSC parent who moved to Oregon after retiring. David mentored us on how to do tasks such as sawing lumber, nailing sheets of metal, and measuring posts and beams that allowed us to create a wooden shed to protect firewood from the unpredictable Oregon weather. The crew members saw sun, rain, hail, and the most gorgeous and magnificent double rainbow all in one day. The weather changed faster than California weather. Besides construction work, the crew engaged in multiple fun activities like throwing disks on the nearby disk golf course, playing ping pong on two picnic tables shoved together, exploring the forests to visit waterfalls, getting to know the nearby farm animals, including Millie the Goat, and going to see Come From Away at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival, a moving play about a close-knit community that came together to support passengers rerouted to the small Canadian town of Gander during 9/11. articles.text: Piedmont Roundup Market Observations, Insider Wisdom & The Week in Piedmont Real Estate Measure H, the proposed sequel to Piedmont’s school parcel tax, is hitting the June 2 ballot. For homeowners weighing their vote—and buyers crunching the numbers on carrying costs— it’s time to peel back the curtain on how this differs from the Measure G we already know. While the framework feels familiar, two specific tweaks in the fine print deserve a closer look. The annual growth cap. Measure G kept the tax rate hike on a leash of 2 percent per year. Measure H bumps that ceiling to 3 percent. It might not sound like much on day one, but thanks to compounding, those extra points can lead to larger bills down the road. The sunset clause. Measure G comes with an expiration date, forcing the school district to come back and ask for permission every few years. Measure H, however, is a forever tax; it has no sunset clause and stays on the books until voters actively move to repeal it. In the News: Pool Parking Pushback From very smart young journalists at The Highlander comes a well put together parking pushback. When will municipal government learn that revolutions are built on inconvenienced citizens? Piedmont’s pool parking, which is near Piedmont’s schools, is already drawing pushback from students, and the complaints are not hard to understand. The city converted 30 spaces to two-hour parking and stepped-up enforcement, which means fewer longterm spots for PHS, MHS, and PMS students and staff. The Highlander editorial argues the result will be more tardies, more tickets, and more frustration for teachers who already deal with limited parking. It also notes that the new pool does not justify making weekday school parking worse, especially when swim and water polo practices themselves run about two hours. The bigger issue is process. Students say many only learned about the changes after getting ticketed, and a student petition to reverse the decision quickly gathered hundreds of signatures. If you want people to support civic change, start by not making their daily lives harder. While the framework feels Piedmont Roundup: Measure H, pool parking and the April market familiar, two specific tweaks in the fine print deserve a closer look. The annual growth cap. Measure G kept the tax rate hike on a leash of 2 percent per year. Measure H bumps that ceiling to 3 percent. It might not sound like much on day one, but thanks to compounding, those extra points can lead to larger bills down the road. The sunset clause. Measure G comes with an expiration date, forcing the school district to come back and ask for permission every few years. Measure H, however, is a forever tax; it has no sunset clause and stays on the books until voters actively move to repeal it. In the News: Pool Parking Pushback From very smart young journalists at The Highlander comes a well put together parking pushback. When will municipal government learn that revolutions are built on inconvenienced citizens? Piedmont’s pool parking, which is near Piedmont’s schools, is already drawing pushback from students, and the complaints are not hard to understand. The city converted 30 spaces to two-hour parking and stepped-up enforcement, which means fewer longterm spots for PHS, MHS, and PMS students and staff. The Highlander editorial argues the result will be more tardies, more tickets, and more frustration for teachers who already deal with limited parking. It also notes that the new pool does not justify making weekday school parking worse, especially when swim and water polo practices themselves run about two hours. The bigger issue is process. Students say many only learned about the changes after getting ticketed, and a student petition to reverse the decision quickly gathered hundreds of signatures. If you want people to support civic change, start by not making their daily lives harder. articles.text: Encore performing arts summer camp for adults At a time when the world can feel full of stress and uncertainty, Stagebridge offers a much-needed burst of joy. Whether participants come for clowning, storytelling, singing around the piano, or the simple pleasure of trying something new, they will find a place alive with laughter, creativity, and connection. This July, Stagebridge will host Encore Performing Arts Summer Camp for adults, a weeklong immersion in improv, clowning, storytelling, singing, tap dancing, and more. Students spend the week learning, playing, and creating across disciplines, making Summer Camp one of Stagebridge’s most community-building events of the year. This year’s offerings include returning favorites in acting, singing, and clowning, along with new options such as drumming and Storytelling as Resistance. Participants choose one morning session and one afternoon session for the week, which culminates in a community showcase for family and friends. A sense of belonging is woven through the Stagebridge experience. Students come to learn a craft, but often leave with something deeper: a strong sense of belonging. “The stories we tell make me feel closer to my community,” said Jason Donchin, a student in Stagebridge’s storytelling program. Breakfast and lunch are included each day, giving participants time to socialize between classes in the light- and plantfilled halls of Stagebridge’s beautiful 100-year-old home. Located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, inside the First Congregational Church of Oakland, Stagebridge is just across from Lake Merritt’s Whole Foods and a short walk from the 19th Street BART station and just steps from the bus line 33. Stagebridge is dedicated to lifelong learners ages 50 and up, with classes and events that celebrate the voices, perspectives, and experiences of older adults. Whether someone is stepping into the spotlight for the first time or returning to a long-loved creative practice, Stagebridge provides a welcoming place to grow, explore, and rediscover the joy of expression. articles.text: There’s a quiet truth about aging that we don’t talk about enough: more people are doing it alone than ever before. In fact, nearly 27% of Americans over 60 now live independently. But let’s reframe that right away. Solo doesn’t mean alone. Independent doesn’t mean isolated. Planning ahead isn’t about preparing for the worst. It’s about creating freedom and peace of mind so you can live fully today, travel when you want, enjoy your daily routines, and embrace life without the constant “what if” lingering in the background. If you’re navigating this chapter without nearby family, this guide is for you. These are the essential pillars I share with clients and friends to turn uncertainty into confidence. Health and Medical Directives Start with the documents that speak for you when you can’t. An Advance Health Care Directive outlines your wishes, while a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care names someone to make decisions on your behalf. Add a HIPAA Authorization so trusted individuals can access your medical information. Your healthcare proxy doesn’t need to be family. A close friend, neighbor, or professional fiduciary can step into this role with care and clarity. Keep copies accessible, at home, with your doctor, and with your attorney. Finances Made Simple Think in four words: Automate, Authorize, Organize, Outsource. Automate bills and deposits. Authorize a trusted person as financial power of attorney. Organize your accounts in one place, whether digital or physical. And outsource when needed, a daily money manager or advisor can keep everything running smoothly. This isn’t about giving up control, it’s about protecting your independence. Daily Living and Support Technology has made independent living easier than ever. Grocery delivery, ride services, and meal programs simplify everyday tasks. Concierge services and local senior centers add both convenience and connection. Equally important is building your go-to list: a handyman, gardener, or housekeeper you trust. Having reliable support in place turns small challenges into manageable moments. Legal and Estate Planning Every solo senior should have five key documents: a Living Trust, Will, Letter of Instruction, updated beneficiary designations, and a pet care plan if needed. If family isn’t available to serve as executor or trustee, professionals can step in. This is not a compromise, it’s often a smarter, more neutral solution. Housing and Aging in Place Make your home work for you. Small upgrades, grab bars, better lighting, non-slip surfaces, can extend your independence significantly. Equally important is having a Plan B. Explore future housing options before you need them. When decisions are made from a place of strength, they feel empowering, not overwhelming.* (See my offer below.) Your Chosen Family This may be the most important pillar of all. Identify three people: one for medical decisions, one for financial matters, and one as an emergency contact. These roles can overlap, but clarity is everything. Then expand your circle. Friends, neighbors, community groups, these connections create both safety and joy. A simple daily check-in system can make all the difference. The One Thing That Matters Most If you do nothing else, create an “If Something Happens” folder. articles.text: City of Oakland Business Tax Exemption Shall the measure amending Oakland’s Business Tax Ordinance to provide one-year business tax exemptions for (1) certain small businesses with annual gross receipts of $1,000,000 or less, including retail sales, grocers, business and personal services, recreation and entertainment, and manufacturing, and (2} businesses that establish a new commercial location in the City; and authorizing the City Council to extend the exemptions on an annual basis for up to three additional years, be adopted? Vote Required: 50%+1 Criteria: 1. Intent and structure of tax (i.e. a % or rate for a sales or transfer tax, or a $ per parcel for a parcel tax) 2. Amount of the tax generated per year 3.
